title: Going async: queues in the design
summary: When a queue belongs in the request path and what it costs, queue or log at design level, why consumers beyond the partition count sit idle, and how to size partitions and drain a backlog.

steps.title: Move work out of the request
body: A synchronous chain is only as fast and as available as its slowest, flakiest link. A queue cuts the chain:
```text
sync:   client ──> API ──> payments ──> email ──> search      every hop must be up, now
async:  client ──> API ──> [ queue ] ──> email worker          the API answers 202 Accepted
└────> search indexer        workers catch up at their own pace
Go async when the caller does not need the result to carry on: emails, thumbnails, search updates,
fan-out to followers, analytics. Three things you buy:
- **Decoupling**: email can be down for ten minutes and no order fails.
- **Load levelling**: a spike becomes a backlog that drains later, not a wall of 503s.
- **Fan-out**: one event, many independent consumers.
And the bill: results arrive **later** (the UI must say "processing"), messages are delivered **at least once**
(so duplicates happen), order is only kept per key, and you now run and watch a broker.
The **Messaging** topic covers RabbitMQ and Kafka in depth; here we decide *where* a queue goes and *how big*.

steps.prompt: For an online shop, which work stays in the request and which goes behind a queue?
items: Authorise the card before showing "order placed"
Resize an uploaded photo into thumbnails
Update the search index after a product edit
Fan a new post out to followers' timelines
steps.explain: If the next screen depends on the answer (logged in or not, card accepted or not, the total), keep it in the request. If the user can carry on without it, a queue makes the request faster and protects it from that dependency's outages.

steps.title: Queue or log, at design level
body: | | Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) | Log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar) |
| A message is | work to do, deleted when acked | a record kept for its retention time |
| Many readers | competing consumers share one queue | each consumer group reads everything at its own offset |
| Replay last week | no, it is gone | yes, reset the group's offset |
| Order | per queue, lost with many consumers | per partition (so per key) |
| Scale reads by | adding consumers | adding partitions, then consumers |
Rule of thumb: **tasks** (send this email, resize this photo) fit a queue. **Facts** that several teams read,
or that you may need to replay (orders placed, prices changed), fit a log.
> **Tip:** in a design interview, name which one and say why in one sentence. "Orders go to a log keyed by
> order id, so billing, search and analytics each get a consumer group and we can replay."

steps.prompt: Billing, the search indexer and the analytics team all need every `OrderPlaced` event. Analytics also wants to re-read the last seven days after fixing a bug. What fits best?
options: A log topic with 7+ days of retention and one consumer group per team
One work queue that all three teams consume from
Three queues, with the API publishing to each one
Synchronous HTTP calls from the order API to each team
steps.explain: Competing consumers on one queue would split the events between the teams. Three queues work but cannot replay and make the API know every reader. A log keeps the facts, and each group keeps its own position.

steps.title: Consumers never beat partitions
body: In a log, each partition is read by **at most one consumer per group**. Extra consumers sit idle. So
throughput is capped by the partition count, not the pod count:
```text
active consumers = min(consumers, partitions)
drain rate       = active consumers × rate per consumer
partitions       = max(peak × headroom / per-partition limit,
peak × headroom / per-consumer rate)
Pick the partition count up front with headroom: adding partitions later changes which partition a key
hashes to, which breaks per-key ordering during the switch. Step through ten consumers on six partitions:
the four extra pods do nothing, and the burst still takes two intervals to drain.

steps.prompt: Four partitions, eight consumers, each consumer handles 1,000 messages per interval. What does this print?
steps.explain: Only four consumers can work, so the drain rate is 4,000 per interval. 7,000 arriving leaves 3,000; then 3,000 + 2,000 = 5,000 minus 4,000 leaves 1,000.

prompt: **Symptom first.** The thumbnail pipeline is 40 minutes behind after a marketing push. Someone scaled the
workers from 6 to 12 pods an hour ago and nothing improved. You run:
code: GROUP       TOPIC    PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG     CONSUMER-ID
(6 more members have no partitions assigned)
options: The topic has 6 partitions, so the 6 new pods are idle: raise the partition count (planning for the key remapping) or make each consumer faster
The broker is overloaded: add brokers
The consumers are crashing: look at their logs
Lag is spread evenly, so everything is fine and it will catch up
steps.explain: Six partitions, six members with assignments, six members with none. Lag is even across partitions, so it is a throughput limit, not a hot key or a stuck consumer. More pods cannot help until there are more partitions, or each consumer does more per second (batching, more threads per partition with care for order).

steps.prompt: Match each situation to what the design should do.
pairs: A consumer crashes after writing to the DB but before committing its offset
The message comes again: dedupe on its message id
The queue absorbs it and workers drain at their own rate
Ten consumers, six partitions, lag growing
Four consumers are idle: more partitions or faster consumers
The next screen needs the result
Billing and analytics both need every event
One consumer group each on a log
steps.explain: At-least-once delivery means every consumer must be idempotent (Messaging, Delivery guarantees). Everything else is sizing and choosing the right shape.

steps.title: Fan-out patterns
body: Three shapes cover most designs:
- **Work queue**: N workers compete for tasks. Scale by adding workers. Thumbnails, emails.
- **Publish-subscribe**: one event, a copy per subscriber (an exchange to several queues, or one consumer group
per team on a log). Order placed → billing, search, analytics.
- **Fan-out to users**: one post becomes a write to each follower's timeline. The work is
`posts × followers`, so a celebrity post is millions of writes. *Classic designs* covers fan-out on write
versus on read.
Whatever the shape, **at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer** is the default. Store the message id with
the side effect in one transaction, or make the write naturally idempotent (`UPSERT` by a business key).

steps.title: How many partitions?
prompt: Write `int PartitionsNeeded(int peakPerSec, int perPartitionPerSec, int perConsumerPerSec, double headroom)`:
- the target rate is `peakPerSec × headroom`;
- you need enough partitions for the **partition limit** (`target / perPartitionPerSec`, rounded up)
and enough for the **consumers** to keep up (`target / perConsumerPerSec`, rounded up), because each
partition has at most one consumer;
- return the larger of the two, and **at least 1**;
- `headroom` below `1` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
`PartitionsNeeded(10000, 1000, 500, 1.5)` is `30`: the partitions could take 15, but slow consumers need 30.
starter: int PartitionsNeeded(int peakPerSec, int perPartitionPerSec, int perConsumerPerSec, double headroom)
solution: int PartitionsNeeded(int peakPerSec, int perPartitionPerSec, int perConsumerPerSec, double headroom)
hints: Work in doubles: `var target = peakPerSec * headroom;` then `Math.Ceiling(target / perPartitionPerSec)`.
template: Dojo.Eq("tiny traffic still needs one", 1, PartitionsNeeded(900, 1000, 1000, 1.0));
Dojo.Eq("no traffic: still one partition", 1, PartitionsNeeded(0, 1000, 1000, 2.0));

steps.title: Watch the backlog
prompt: Write `int[] Backlog(int[] arrivals, int partitions, int consumers, int perConsumer)` that returns the backlog
**after** each interval:
- only `min(consumers, partitions)` consumers can work;
- in each interval, add the arrivals, then remove up to `active × perConsumer` messages (never below 0).
Then write `int IntervalsToDrain(int[] arrivals, int partitions, int consumers, int perConsumer)`: the
1-based number of the first interval, **at or after the last interval with arrivals**, whose backlog is 0. If
the backlog is not 0 by then, keep simulating intervals with **no arrivals**. If nothing can ever drain it
(no active consumers and a backlog), return `-1`.
With `{ 3000, 9000, 9000, 3000, 3000 }`, 6 partitions, 10 consumers and 1,000 each: the backlog is
`0, 3000, 6000, 3000, 0` and `IntervalsToDrain` is `5`.
starter: int[] Backlog(int[] arrivals, int partitions, int consumers, int perConsumer)
int IntervalsToDrain(int[] arrivals, int partitions, int consumers, int perConsumer)
solution: int[] Backlog(int[] arrivals, int partitions, int consumers, int perConsumer)
int IntervalsToDrain(int[] arrivals, int partitions, int consumers, int perConsumer)
var levels = Backlog(arrivals, partitions, consumers, perConsumer);
for (var i = 0; i < arrivals.Length; i++) if (arrivals[i] > 0) lastArrival = i;
for (var i = lastArrival; i < levels.Length; i++) if (levels[i] == 0) return i + 1;
hints: `var active = Math.Min(consumers, partitions);` and the same two lines as the trace, storing the backlog each time.
After the arrays run out, each extra interval removes `active × perConsumer`: that is a rounded-up division.
template: Dojo.Eq("the trace: ten consumers, six partitions", new[] { 0, 3000, 6000, 3000, 0 }, Backlog(new[] { 3000, 9000, 9000, 3000, 3000 }, 6, 10, 1000));
Dojo.Eq("more pods than partitions changes nothing", Backlog(new[] { 3000, 9000, 9000 }, 6, 6, 1000), Backlog(new[] { 3000, 9000, 9000 }, 6, 60, 1000));
Dojo.Eq("more partitions with enough pods drain faster", new[] { 0, 0, 0 }, Backlog(new[] { 3000, 9000, 9000 }, 12, 12, 1000));
Dojo.Eq("10,000 at 4,000 per interval: drained in interval 3", 3, IntervalsToDrain(new[] { 10000 }, 4, 4, 1000));
Dojo.Eq("backlog of 6000 at 4000 per interval needs two quiet intervals", 4, IntervalsToDrain(new[] { 0, 10000 }, 2, 2, 2000));
Dojo.Eq("no arrivals at all: already drained", 0, IntervalsToDrain(new[] { 0, 0 }, 4, 4, 1000));

steps.title: Build it: absorb the write burst
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *Absorb the write burst*. A ticket on-sale sends a burst of writes
that the database cannot take synchronously. Put a **queue** and **workers** in the write path so the API
answers 202 quickly, keep the database under its limit, and drain the backlog in time. Remember: workers
beyond the partition count do nothing.
steps.explain: The queue turns a write spike into a backlog, the workers set the pace the database can take, and the partition count caps how many workers can help. The cost is that the user sees "processing" for a little while.
